html:
SMTO-AUT-0004 — The computer didn't accept the administrator password

GUID: e9865b75-f237-43a1-9a72-5089cdb12b45
Slug: credential-rejected
Domain: AUT · Subsystem: aut

What happened

  • SMTO tried to run a command with administrator rights, but the password was refused, either by the computer or because it contained a line break. The command did not run.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Make sure the password belongs to the account the Gateway runs as on that computer, not to your own account somewhere else. The computer only accepts the password of the account SMTO uses to run commands there.
  2. When SMTO asks for the password again, type it on one line, with Caps Lock off and no extra spaces or line breaks. SMTO refuses passwords that contain a line break, and the computer rejects any difference in what you type.
  3. If the password may have changed recently, ask the person who manages that computer to confirm the current one. An old password is refused even when it's typed correctly.

What success looks like

  • The step runs and is marked Elevated, with no password error.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages that computer. Never paste the password into a Task request, a screenshot, or the error report.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Managed sudo elevation failed before the command started: the supplied password contained a newline, carriage return or NUL, sudo's authentication output (for example 'incorrect password' or 'authentication failure') was classified as a rejected credential, or sudo still asked for a password after one was supplied.

What this means

  • The managed elevation path rejects line/NUL characters in a password or classifies sudo authentication output as credential rejection. Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.

Why this can happen

  • The managed elevation path rejects line/NUL characters in a password or classifies sudo authentication output as credential rejection.

How to diagnose it

  • Distinguish local password-format validation from sudo rejection indicators; confirm the selected account before another credential attempt.

How to fix it

  • Verify the account (the Gateway process user or the verified SSH user) and that the sudo password is a single line; check the host's authentication log (for example /var/log/auth.log or journalctl) for the sudo failure. Re-supply the corrected password only through the private ask_user/sudo_password flow, never in task text, command arguments or diagnostics.
  • Correct the credential through the existing private authentication flow; check account and format before another attempt. Never paste it into diagnostics.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • A supported private credential is accepted for the intended account and elevation is confirmed.

What not to do

  • Do not put credentials in task text, command arguments, screenshots or diagnostic reports.

Technical notes

  • Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
